fatal_errors: The proposed lattice-distortion-driven dynamic-recovery mechanism is not supported by the reported evidence and partly conflicts with the paper's interpretation of lattice distortion as a source of strengthening and frictional resistance.
The hypothesis replaces the actual as-cast, segregated two-BCC-phase microstructure and coarse powder-sintered tungsten baseline with hypothetical homogenized, grain-size-matched materials.
The proposed 500–1000 °C tensile and creep regime does not reconstruct the reported room-temperature compression, room-temperature-to-500 °C indentation, and room-temperature scratch experiments.
No prior evidence or citations support the central causal assignment.
explanation: The response correctly predicts greater plastic deformation and toughness than pure tungsten and proposes potentially useful in-situ measurements. However, it does not reconstruct the studied materials or tests. The target alloy was an as-cast, dendritically segregated two-BCC-phase material, whereas the response assumes homogenization and matched microstructures. Its dynamic-recovery mechanism was not measured in the target study; the reported interpretation instead associated lattice distortion and W/Ta frictional resistance mainly with strength, while improved damage tolerance was tentatively linked to Ti, V, and Zr effects, localized plasticity, grain-boundary cohesion, and crack impediment. The experiment could test a new alternative mechanism, but comparing two different compositions alone would not isolate lattice distortion without additional HEA controls or direct quantitative recovery measurements. The falsification rule also conflates failure to improve macroscopic properties with failure of the specific recovery mechanism.
